name: Sapphire Blue
lede: Sapphire Blue is a deep, saturated blue named for the gem, and the gem's own name once meant a different stone.

sections.title: The stone with a shifting name
sections.body:
The ancients' *sapphirus* was not today's blue corundum; it was lapis lazuli, and that lasted until well into the middle of the 13th century [1]. The adjective *saphirinus* described dark, opaque things, including Frisian felts, not clear light blue [1]. So "sapphire blue" has meant different blues at different times [1].

Early recipe texts use the phrase for dye colors too: a text quoted in the Pigment Compendium describes three kinds of *folium*, a plant dye, one purple, one red and one sapphire blue, and Theophilus, writing about the 12th century, also describes the three [2]. Paterson adds that Berlin blue is sometimes a lighter sapphire blue [3]. See [[lapis-lazuli]], [[royal-blue]] and [[prussian-blue]] for relatives [1][3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 28 hold this color at 5% of the canvas or more, as photographed [4]. One is Van Gogh's 1888 *Three White Cottages in Saintes-Maries* [4].

origin.named_after: the gem sapphire, whose ancient name meant lapis lazuli
origin.first_recorded: folium kinds described in a medieval recipe text; Theophilus c. 12th century

questions.q: What did the ancient word sapphirus usually mean?
True or false: the ancients' sapphire was today's blue corundum.

openers: The ancients' sapphire was lapis lazuli, not the blue gem we call sapphire today.
Sapphire blue also named a plant dye, folium, in medieval recipes.

issues: Tightened date wording to Gage's 'middle of the thirteenth century'; Theophilus described the three folium colors, not necessarily the phrase.
